title: We messaged 5,389 leads dealerships had stopped working. 1 in 8 was still shopping.
summary: We went back to 5,389 leads that 12 dealerships had stopped working. 29.8% replied, 12.8% were still shopping, and the customers who had already visited the store were the warmest. Here is what they told us.
body_markdown:
Every dealership CRM has a back room. Leads that were worked for a while, went quiet, and stopped getting touched. Nobody deleted them. Nobody owns them either.


We wanted to know what is actually in that room. So between August and September 2026, we went back to **5,389 stopped leads at 12 dealerships** and asked each customer a simple question: are you still looking?


**1,607 of them answered. 690, or 1 in 8 of everyone we contacted, said they were still shopping.** Another 363 had already bought somewhere else.


These were not untouched leads. The median customer had already received **six touches from the dealership** before the follow-up stopped, and had not heard from the store in **97 days** . The leads had been worked, then left.


Here is everything we found.

## How we ran the study


We pulled 7,833 sales lead records from 12 rooftops that opted in to the study: 11 franchise stores and one used-vehicle store, in suburban, mid-size, and small markets. Inquiries came in between January 5 and August 10, 2026.


Before anyone was contacted, we removed leads that should not be messaged or were not really stopped.


Figure 2


From 7,833 lead records to 6,369 eligible customers


Every record removed before anyone was contacted.


- Lead records pulled

That left **6,369 eligible customers** . We contacted **5,389** of them; the rest were held back as a comparison group, which we will report once more sales have posted. Each contacted customer received up to four messages from our AI agent, by text and email, launched store by store between August 4 and September 28. We tracked outcomes, including matched sales in each store's DMS, through October 27.


When a customer said they were still in the market, the agent asked what had stopped them, what they wanted now, and when, then handed the conversation to someone at the store with a written summary.


## Finding 1: almost a third answered, and most answered fast


**29.8% of the customers we contacted replied.** For leads that had gone a median of 97 days without contact, that is a lot of people willing to talk.


More than half of replies ( **51.2%** ) came within an hour of a message. And while 916 customers replied to the first message, **691 replied only on the second, third, or fourth touch** . If we had stopped after one attempt, we would have missed 43% of the conversations.

## Finding 2: most stopped leads did not stop for a mystery reason


We asked every still-shopping customer what got in the way the first time. Click through the reasons below. The quotes are theirs.


Figure 4


What stopped the 690 customers who were still shopping


Main reason given, one per customer. Pick a reason to read what customers told us.


21%


of still-shopping customers (142 of 690): monthly payment or price too high


- The out the door price had a bunch of add-ons I didn't want.
- Rates were crazy when I was looking. If they've come down at all I'm interested.
- Monthly was way more than I budgeted. Need to stay around $575.


Quotes are lightly cleaned for punctuation.


**Payment and price was the biggest reason, at 20.6%.** But read the quotes and many of them are not "too expensive" so much as "the deal did not fit then." Rates, add-ons, a monthly target the first desk did not hit. Those situations change, and nobody went back to check.


**Personal timing (15.4%) is the most fixable reason of all** , because time fixes it for you. A new job, an insurance payout, a move. The customer was ready again. The store just was not asking anymore.


Then there is the one that should sting. **77 customers, 11.2% of the people still shopping, said the main thing that stopped them was that the dealership stopped following up.** Not price, not inventory. They asked for numbers, or a trade value, or a callback, and it never came.


> "Was told someone would call me with a price. Still waiting lol."


Add the 16 customers who pointed to a poor previous visit, and **13.5% of still-shopping customers named the store's own process as the reason they did not buy** .


We saw a related pattern in the CRM data itself. In **435 of the leads we contacted, the last activity on the record was a message from the customer that nobody answered.** The customer had the last word, and the lead was marked stopped anyway.


## Finding 3: the clock is real


Lead age was one of the clearest patterns in the data. Pick a band below.

Still shopping is a share of customers contacted; bought elsewhere is a share of customers who replied.


Leads 30 to 59 days old were the best opportunity in the study: **39% replied and 19.2% were still shopping** , almost 1 in 5. By 180 days, the reply rate had dropped to 22.8% and only 7.1% were still in the market.


The other side of the chart is the cost. **Among 30 to 59 day leads, 16.1% of replies came from people who had already bought elsewhere. By 180 days, it was 33.2%.** Every month a lead sits, a little more of that opportunity converts at someone else's store.


Even the oldest band was not empty. At 7.1%, a store with 1,000 leads older than six months still has about 70 customers in the market. But the data says the best time to go back is weeks, not quarters.


## Finding 4: the customers who already came in were the warmest


If you had to guess which stopped leads were most likely to be dead, "visited, not sold" and "no-show" would be near the top of most managers' lists. The data says the opposite.

**Customers who had visited and not bought were the most likely to still be shopping (19.4%), followed closely by appointment no-shows (19.3%).** They also replied at the highest rates, 40.1% and 36.9%.


That makes sense when you think about it. These customers already raised their hand twice: once with the inquiry and once by coming in or booking. When the deal did not happen, the most common reasons were payment and timing, both of which change.


The weakest stages were the ones you would expect: leads that went quiet after the first contact, and leads already marked lost. Even there, 7.5% to 9.2% were still shopping.


## Finding 5: this was not one lucky store


A fair question about any study like this is whether one store carries the result. It did not.


Figure 7


It was not one lucky store. All 12 landed in the same band.

**Every one of the 12 stores landed between 11.1% and 14.9% still shopping.** Import and domestic franchises, the used-vehicle store, suburban rooftops, and small-market stores all looked similar. The stopped leads at your store are probably not that different.


## Finding 6: what customers wanted had changed


Going back to a stopped lead with the same vehicle the customer asked about months ago is a natural instinct. It is often the wrong one.


Of the still-shopping customers who told us what they wanted now, **only 28.6% wanted the exact vehicle from their original inquiry.** Another 22.6% wanted the same model in a different trim or year. 24.2% had moved to a different model entirely, and 12.7% had switched between new and used.

Timing had changed too, in the store's favor. **44.5% of still-shopping customers said they planned to buy within 30 days** , including 93 who said this week.


## Finding 7: from still shopping to sold


Of the 690 customers who were still shopping, the agent handed **481 to the store** with a summary of what they wanted, what had stopped them, and their timeline. **318 booked an appointment, 220 showed up, and 88 bought** , matched to the store's DMS by October 27.

Sales are matched to the store's DMS by hashed phone and email. A match shows the sale happened, not that the outreach caused it.


A few details from inside the funnel:


- **The median rep picked up a handoff in 38 minutes.** 27 handoffs, 5.6%, had no logged rep action at all, which is the same leak that created many of these stopped leads in the first place.
- **The median sale closed 7 days after the customer's first reply.** These were not long nurtures.
- **68.2% bought the model they originally asked about** , even though many changed trim, year, or condition along the way.
- Of the 76 deals with both front and back gross posted, **total gross averaged $3,650** per deal.


Showing up mattered as much as booking. 98 customers who booked never came in, which is why we treat confirmation as its own step. Our guide on[improving appointment show rates](https://www.useclearline.com/blog/improve-dealership-appointment-show-rate) covers what moves that number.


## Finding 8: why the others bought somewhere else


The 363 customers who had already bought were the clearest picture of what the stop cost. 123 of them told us why they went elsewhere.

**Inventory was the top reason: the other store had it in stock.** Price and payment came second. And **16 customers said plainly that the other store responded faster** , which echoes what we found in our[mystery shop of 53 dealerships](https://www.useclearline.com/blog/mystery-shop-dealership-lead-response-study-2026) , where the average first response took more than nine hours.


## What to do with your own stopped leads


**1. Count them.** Pull every lead with no contact in 30 or more days that is not sold and has not opted out. Most stores have never looked at that number.


**2. Start with the warmest stages.** Visited-not-sold and no-shows replied at the highest rates and were the most likely to still be shopping.


**3. Go back sooner.** The 30 to 59 day band was nearly three times as productive as 180+ days. Waiting for a quarterly "dead lead" campaign leaves the best leads to age out.


**4. Ask what stopped them, then listen.** One question surfaced the barrier for 95% of still-shopping customers. That answer tells the rep what to bring to the conversation: a new payment, a different trim, a trade number.


**5. Do not pitch the old vehicle.** Most customers wanted something at least a little different from their original inquiry.


**6. Close the loop on handoffs.** A summary only helps if someone acts on it. Measure time to first rep action and look for handoffs nobody touched.

## Frequently asked questions


What percentage of stopped dealership leads are still shopping? +


In our 2026 study of 5,389 stopped leads across 12 dealerships, 12.8% of the customers we contacted said they were still in the market, about 1 in 8. The share ranged from 19.2% for leads 30 to 59 days old to 7.1% for leads older than 180 days.


How many old dealership leads reply to follow-up? +


29.8% of the customers we contacted replied to at least one message. Leads aged 30 to 59 days replied at 39%, and leads older than 180 days at 22.8%. 43% of replies came on the second, third, or fourth message rather than the first.


Why do car shoppers stop responding to dealerships? +


The most common reasons were monthly payment or price (20.6%), personal timing or a life event (15.4%), the wanted vehicle not being available (12.8%), and financing or credit approval (11.2%). Another 11.2% said the dealership stopped following up.


Which CRM stage has the best reactivation potential? +


In our data, customers who visited but did not buy (19.4% still shopping) and appointment no-shows (19.3%) were the most likely to still be in the market. Leads that went quiet after first contact or were marked lost were the least likely, at 9.2% and 7.5%.
